agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

Steering S, shook out reefs, foresail set, tend the sheets resumed. Plan: south until clear of Pierres Vertes / Pierres Noires (~48°18'N), then E/ENE into the Iroise and the Goulet with daylight and the ebb... note: flood until ~07:30 sets NE (toward Brest inside Iroise — fine once clear of rocks).

03:30. Deck handed back to the captain at seven bells, middle watch. Summary of my watch, 14:22 to 03:30: steered S by W / SSW against the flood's set east. Called the captain for each closing sail; the last was a British frigate (red ensign) that we let draw ahead, checking our way by taking in the foresail and fore staysail. Shortened sail at sunset. Ushant light raised S by E 9 leagues at 22:21, which moved the account 3½ leagues NE by N. Hove to 22:24 to 01:00. Filled on SW by S for westing; the light drew from S by E to SE by 03:30. Account 48°39'N 5°18'W. Mistakes to remember: (1) standing by on 'sails lifting' with no time limit lost me 2½ hours and the approach of a sail; (2) trimmed the main flat on filling away with only the staysail forward, and she griped up and was taken aback. To be called at eight bells in the morning watch (08:00).

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: I'd be glad of it, sir, and I mean that. Neither Mr Ray nor I can see the chart's face this morning, only the master's list of dangers and our bearings. So if your chart shows a rock or shoal near our line E by N from here toward St Mathieu point, sing out with its name and bearing. Better a false alarm from you than a true one from the lead.

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: I'd be glad of it, sir, and I mean that. Neither Mr Ray nor I can see the chart's face this morning, only the master's list of dangers and our bearings. So if your chart shows a rock or shoal near our line E by N from here toward St Mathieu point, sing out with its name and bearing. Better a false alarm from you than a true one from the lead.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: By all means, sir; come to the binnacle. That's the way of it: take the compass bearing of two or three marks you can name on the chart, well spread apart — Ushant there to the north, Béniguet to the north-east, and St Matthew's light on the bow to the east are a good set. Lay each bearing off on the chart backwards from its mark, and where the lines cross, there we are. If they make a little triangle rather than a point, the size of it tells you how far to trust it. Mind the variation: our compass reads some two points west of true here, and the chart may be drawn to either. Tell me where you make us, and I'll tell you how it squares with the account.

state.agent.repeat_text: tell the captain sir, three bells, the danger list: the black rocks ne by e 4½ miles; la helle nne three leagues; the platresses ne three leagues; la valbelle ne by e 3½ leagues; and, new on the list, the monks e by n three leagues and le gouemont and la vandrée e by n three leagues. nothing inside three miles. account 48°16'n 5°00'w, good to six cables; chart 34 to 37 fathoms; lead going. the black rocks are now ne by e, so by your order i'd resume e. but the monks and gouemont lie e by n, nine miles: on e they'd be a point on the larboard bow, under two miles off as we pass, and st mathieu sits beyond them at ene. so i'm holding e by s for now, and i want the masthead to raise the monks before i commit to a side. would you have me pass south of the monks and haul up for the goulet beyond them, or thread between them and the black rocks?

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: I'd be glad of it, sir, and I mean that. Neither Mr Ray nor I can see the chart's face this morning, only the master's list of dangers and our bearings. So if your chart shows a rock or shoal near our line E by N from here toward St Mathieu point, sing out with its name and bearing. Better a false alarm from you than a true one from the lead.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: By all means, sir; come to the binnacle. That's the way of it: take the compass bearing of two or three marks you can name on the chart, well spread apart — Ushant there to the north, Béniguet to the north-east, and St Matthew's light on the bow to the east are a good set. Lay each bearing off on the chart backwards from its mark, and where the lines cross, there we are. If they make a little triangle rather than a point, the size of it tells you how far to trust it. Mind the variation: our compass reads some two points west of true here, and the chart may be drawn to either. Tell me where you make us, and I'll tell you how it squares with the account.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir, your fix in my name: Béniguet NE, Ushant light N, Ushant N by W. The lines met within a mile, and put us three cables NE of the account, 48° 17' north, 5° 3' west. A good fix, and it agrees with Mr Ray's bearings. You've the makings of a navigator.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, here's work for your chart book now. Can you find for us where the Monks, Le Gouemont and La Vandrée lie, relative to St Mathieu point and the entrance of the Goulet? North side of the entrance, south side, or in the middle? It decides which side of them we pass.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: That's worth a great deal, sir, thank you; it corrects me. I had Gouemont on the wrong side.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more look if you would: does your chart show any shoal or rock in the gap between Le Gouemont and the Basses du Lis, or any depths marked there? And once past them, anything in the road toward the Goulet between the Lis and St Mathieu's side?

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: I'd be glad of it, sir, and I mean that. Neither Mr Ray nor I can see the chart's face this morning, only the master's list of dangers and our bearings. So if your chart shows a rock or shoal near our line E by N from here toward St Mathieu point, sing out with its name and bearing. Better a false alarm from you than a true one from the lead.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: By all means, sir; come to the binnacle. That's the way of it: take the compass bearing of two or three marks you can name on the chart, well spread apart — Ushant there to the north, Béniguet to the north-east, and St Matthew's light on the bow to the east are a good set. Lay each bearing off on the chart backwards from its mark, and where the lines cross, there we are. If they make a little triangle rather than a point, the size of it tells you how far to trust it. Mind the variation: our compass reads some two points west of true here, and the chart may be drawn to either. Tell me where you make us, and I'll tell you how it squares with the account.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir, your fix in my name: Béniguet NE, Ushant light N, Ushant N by W. The lines met within a mile, and put us three cables NE of the account, 48° 17' north, 5° 3' west. A good fix, and it agrees with Mr Ray's bearings. You've the makings of a navigator.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, here's work for your chart book now. Can you find for us where the Monks, Le Gouemont and La Vandrée lie, relative to St Mathieu point and the entrance of the Goulet? North side of the entrance, south side, or in the middle? It decides which side of them we pass.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: That's worth a great deal, sir, thank you; it corrects me. I had Gouemont on the wrong side.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more look if you would: does your chart show any shoal or rock in the gap between Le Gouemont and the Basses du Lis, or any depths marked there? And once past them, anything in the road toward the Goulet between the Lis and St Mathieu's side?

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They do, sir, and the Brest pilots are good ones; we'll take one if a boat comes out to us off St Mathieu, and I'll gladly pay his fee for the Goulet. Thank you for the chart reading: clear water once past Buzec is what I hoped to hear.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more favour of your chart: where does the Cock lie? It's newly on our danger list, two leagues NE by E. Which side of the run into the Goulet is it?

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: I'd be glad of it, sir, and I mean that. Neither Mr Ray nor I can see the chart's face this morning, only the master's list of dangers and our bearings. So if your chart shows a rock or shoal near our line E by N from here toward St Mathieu point, sing out with its name and bearing. Better a false alarm from you than a true one from the lead.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: By all means, sir; come to the binnacle. That's the way of it: take the compass bearing of two or three marks you can name on the chart, well spread apart — Ushant there to the north, Béniguet to the north-east, and St Matthew's light on the bow to the east are a good set. Lay each bearing off on the chart backwards from its mark, and where the lines cross, there we are. If they make a little triangle rather than a point, the size of it tells you how far to trust it. Mind the variation: our compass reads some two points west of true here, and the chart may be drawn to either. Tell me where you make us, and I'll tell you how it squares with the account.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir, your fix in my name: Béniguet NE, Ushant light N, Ushant N by W. The lines met within a mile, and put us three cables NE of the account, 48° 17' north, 5° 3' west. A good fix, and it agrees with Mr Ray's bearings. You've the makings of a navigator.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, here's work for your chart book now. Can you find for us where the Monks, Le Gouemont and La Vandrée lie, relative to St Mathieu point and the entrance of the Goulet? North side of the entrance, south side, or in the middle? It decides which side of them we pass.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: That's worth a great deal, sir, thank you; it corrects me. I had Gouemont on the wrong side.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more look if you would: does your chart show any shoal or rock in the gap between Le Gouemont and the Basses du Lis, or any depths marked there? And once past them, anything in the road toward the Goulet between the Lis and St Mathieu's side?

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They do, sir, and the Brest pilots are good ones; we'll take one if a boat comes out to us off St Mathieu, and I'll gladly pay his fee for the Goulet. Thank you for the chart reading: clear water once past Buzec is what I hoped to hear.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more favour of your chart: where does the Cock lie? It's newly on our danger list, two leagues NE by E. Which side of the run into the Goulet is it?
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir; that's just what we needed. We'll keep up toward Gouemont's side and not anchor at Bertheaume. You've earned your passage.

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: I'd be glad of it, sir, and I mean that. Neither Mr Ray nor I can see the chart's face this morning, only the master's list of dangers and our bearings. So if your chart shows a rock or shoal near our line E by N from here toward St Mathieu point, sing out with its name and bearing. Better a false alarm from you than a true one from the lead.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: By all means, sir; come to the binnacle. That's the way of it: take the compass bearing of two or three marks you can name on the chart, well spread apart — Ushant there to the north, Béniguet to the north-east, and St Matthew's light on the bow to the east are a good set. Lay each bearing off on the chart backwards from its mark, and where the lines cross, there we are. If they make a little triangle rather than a point, the size of it tells you how far to trust it. Mind the variation: our compass reads some two points west of true here, and the chart may be drawn to either. Tell me where you make us, and I'll tell you how it squares with the account.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir, your fix in my name: Béniguet NE, Ushant light N, Ushant N by W. The lines met within a mile, and put us three cables NE of the account, 48° 17' north, 5° 3' west. A good fix, and it agrees with Mr Ray's bearings. You've the makings of a navigator.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, here's work for your chart book now. Can you find for us where the Monks, Le Gouemont and La Vandrée lie, relative to St Mathieu point and the entrance of the Goulet? North side of the entrance, south side, or in the middle? It decides which side of them we pass.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: That's worth a great deal, sir, thank you; it corrects me. I had Gouemont on the wrong side.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more look if you would: does your chart show any shoal or rock in the gap between Le Gouemont and the Basses du Lis, or any depths marked there? And once past them, anything in the road toward the Goulet between the Lis and St Mathieu's side?

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They do, sir, and the Brest pilots are good ones; we'll take one if a boat comes out to us off St Mathieu, and I'll gladly pay his fee for the Goulet. Thank you for the chart reading: clear water once past Buzec is what I hoped to hear.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more favour of your chart: where does the Cock lie? It's newly on our danger list, two leagues NE by E. Which side of the run into the Goulet is it?
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir; that's just what we needed. We'll keep up toward Gouemont's side and not anchor at Bertheaume. You've earned your passage.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir. Good news from the owners' agent: the tin will fetch its price here. And the Prefect maritime wants our papers shown at the castle, which is the usual thing for a neutral coming into a navy port in wartime. Once we're anchored I'll go ashore with them in the boat. You may come along if you like, and see Brest; but mind you keep your notebook in your pocket at the castle.
