agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: I'd be glad of it, sir, and I mean that. Neither Mr Ray nor I can see the chart's face this morning, only the master's list of dangers and our bearings. So if your chart shows a rock or shoal near our line E by N from here toward St Mathieu point, sing out with its name and bearing. Better a false alarm from you than a true one from the lead.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: By all means, sir; come to the binnacle. That's the way of it: take the compass bearing of two or three marks you can name on the chart, well spread apart — Ushant there to the north, Béniguet to the north-east, and St Matthew's light on the bow to the east are a good set. Lay each bearing off on the chart backwards from its mark, and where the lines cross, there we are. If they make a little triangle rather than a point, the size of it tells you how far to trust it. Mind the variation: our compass reads some two points west of true here, and the chart may be drawn to either. Tell me where you make us, and I'll tell you how it squares with the account.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir, your fix in my name: Béniguet NE, Ushant light N, Ushant N by W. The lines met within a mile, and put us three cables NE of the account, 48° 17' north, 5° 3' west. A good fix, and it agrees with Mr Ray's bearings. You've the makings of a navigator.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, here's work for your chart book now. Can you find for us where the Monks, Le Gouemont and La Vandrée lie, relative to St Mathieu point and the entrance of the Goulet? North side of the entrance, south side, or in the middle? It decides which side of them we pass.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: That's worth a great deal, sir, thank you; it corrects me. I had Gouemont on the wrong side.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more look if you would: does your chart show any shoal or rock in the gap between Le Gouemont and the Basses du Lis, or any depths marked there? And once past them, anything in the road toward the Goulet between the Lis and St Mathieu's side?

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They do, sir, and the Brest pilots are good ones; we'll take one if a boat comes out to us off St Mathieu, and I'll gladly pay his fee for the Goulet. Thank you for the chart reading: clear water once past Buzec is what I hoped to hear.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more favour of your chart: where does the Cock lie? It's newly on our danger list, two leagues NE by E. Which side of the run into the Goulet is it?
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir; that's just what we needed. We'll keep up toward Gouemont's side and not anchor at Bertheaume. You've earned your passage.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir. Good news from the owners' agent: the tin will fetch its price here. And the Prefect maritime wants our papers shown at the castle, which is the usual thing for a neutral coming into a navy port in wartime. Once we're anchored I'll go ashore with them in the boat. You may come along if you like, and see Brest; but mind you keep your notebook in your pocket at the castle.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: You heard me a touch wrong, sir, though your instinct's right. I said steer toward Petit Minou, to haul her up the north side, and leave the Mingan and the Fillettes to starboard. Petit Minou itself goes to larboard: we pass between it and the Mingan, half a mile or so off the north shore, just as you say. Right now she's making good ENE, which points at the Mingan, so I've hauled her up as close as she'll lie to work north. Keep that chart handy, sir. If you see the Mingan come on our larboard bow, sing out.

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: I'd be glad of it, sir, and I mean that. Neither Mr Ray nor I can see the chart's face this morning, only the master's list of dangers and our bearings. So if your chart shows a rock or shoal near our line E by N from here toward St Mathieu point, sing out with its name and bearing. Better a false alarm from you than a true one from the lead.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: By all means, sir; come to the binnacle. That's the way of it: take the compass bearing of two or three marks you can name on the chart, well spread apart — Ushant there to the north, Béniguet to the north-east, and St Matthew's light on the bow to the east are a good set. Lay each bearing off on the chart backwards from its mark, and where the lines cross, there we are. If they make a little triangle rather than a point, the size of it tells you how far to trust it. Mind the variation: our compass reads some two points west of true here, and the chart may be drawn to either. Tell me where you make us, and I'll tell you how it squares with the account.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir, your fix in my name: Béniguet NE, Ushant light N, Ushant N by W. The lines met within a mile, and put us three cables NE of the account, 48° 17' north, 5° 3' west. A good fix, and it agrees with Mr Ray's bearings. You've the makings of a navigator.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, here's work for your chart book now. Can you find for us where the Monks, Le Gouemont and La Vandrée lie, relative to St Mathieu point and the entrance of the Goulet? North side of the entrance, south side, or in the middle? It decides which side of them we pass.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: That's worth a great deal, sir, thank you; it corrects me. I had Gouemont on the wrong side.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more look if you would: does your chart show any shoal or rock in the gap between Le Gouemont and the Basses du Lis, or any depths marked there? And once past them, anything in the road toward the Goulet between the Lis and St Mathieu's side?

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They do, sir, and the Brest pilots are good ones; we'll take one if a boat comes out to us off St Mathieu, and I'll gladly pay his fee for the Goulet. Thank you for the chart reading: clear water once past Buzec is what I hoped to hear.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more favour of your chart: where does the Cock lie? It's newly on our danger list, two leagues NE by E. Which side of the run into the Goulet is it?
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir; that's just what we needed. We'll keep up toward Gouemont's side and not anchor at Bertheaume. You've earned your passage.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir. Good news from the owners' agent: the tin will fetch its price here. And the Prefect maritime wants our papers shown at the castle, which is the usual thing for a neutral coming into a navy port in wartime. Once we're anchored I'll go ashore with them in the boat. You may come along if you like, and see Brest; but mind you keep your notebook in your pocket at the castle.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: You heard me a touch wrong, sir, though your instinct's right. I said steer toward Petit Minou, to haul her up the north side, and leave the Mingan and the Fillettes to starboard. Petit Minou itself goes to larboard: we pass between it and the Mingan, half a mile or so off the north shore, just as you say. Right now she's making good ENE, which points at the Mingan, so I've hauled her up as close as she'll lie to work north. Keep that chart handy, sir. If you see the Mingan come on our larboard bow, sing out.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir, you're quite right and I had it backwards. Fillettes to starboard, Mingan to larboard, the castle kept open of Penaleuch.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir. We're splitting it as you say: E, between the pilot's two warnings. Keep your chart on it and call out if you see us closing either side.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir. You may well be right, and it's the pilot's two warnings that bear you out: first the Fillettes ahead, deep water to starboard, then the shore ahead, deep water to larboard. Between the two we're in the narrow cable you describe. I'm splitting them now and watching for the next call. If the Fillettes come onto the starboard bow, I'll haul up hard for the Mingan side as you say.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, we've touched on the Fillettes, as your chart warned we might. The fault is mine as master. The flood is rising and she should lift off in a little while; we'll anchor the moment she floats. Stay aft by the taffrail, out of the hands' way, if you'd be so good.

note.text: 13:39 Brought up off the Fillettes/south shore of the Goulet: best bower 100 fm backed by stream, small bower 40 fm, sheet anchor 22 fm; 7 fm, rock and mud; land a cable astern E. Struck the Fillettes 13:03, afloat 13:29; carpenter reported her stove (no pump model). Plan: weigh at slack near HW (~16:15-16:30), go in to the Bay of Brest with the pilot, then show papers at the castle and sell the tin. Lessons: I gave conflicting helm orders in the narrows and twice had the Fillettes' side wrong; I should have heeded the passenger's chart and the pilot sooner, or anchored in Bertheaume to wait.

agent.told: The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Good morning to you, sir. She lies snug in Carrick Road, riding to the best bower in nine and a half fathom, a fine westerly breeze and a clear sky. I've just bought forty-five ton of tin at a hundred and twenty pound; the boat's gone for it. Once it's aboard we weigh for Brest, and with this wind on the beam she'll make a handsome run of it.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They're a good lot, sir — Mr Ray drives them and Mr Paul knows every rope. We're clearing the Old Wall now; once she's an offing from St Anthony we'll bear up for Brest and give her every stitch she'll carry. A hundred miles, and with this breeze we should raise Ushant by tomorrow's dawn.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Ha! The very book. Much obliged, sir — I'll not ask how it came to your cabin. Mr Ray will keep the night by it. A pity it was written for a ship with royals; I've struck those lines and put in our own. You'll see the Lizard lights away to the south-west there, four leagues off.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: She's a sweet thing on a reach, sir: topsail and t'gallant drawing, fore-and-main full, gaff topsail and three headsails pulling, eight knots and dry as a parlour with the wind just forward of the beam. Not a stitch more she could use on this point of sail. (A word aside, out of the game: the ship_view picture came to me as a blank white frame, so I am speaking from the readings, not the picture.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, a correction: I should not have said blank white frame. The ship_view call returned only its catalogue line to me and no picture at all, so I could not see her as you do; what I said of her sails is from the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: thank you. With facing 90 the picture does come through now, but it is an entirely blank white frame, 1568 by 643, with no ship drawn in it. My first try, without a facing, gave me no picture at all, only its catalogue line; I was wrong to call that one a blank frame. So the viewer may not be drawing for the API door. My description of her stands on the readings.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I must correct myself again, plainly: the facing-90 call also returned only its text line, no picture reached me at all. I had no grounds to describe it as a blank white frame; the size I quoted is just what the line says. I'm sorry for the muddle. Either the image is not being passed through to me, or it is shelved before I see it.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside: the chart comes through well — I can see the Lizard peninsula, the Manacles two and a half miles on our starboard quarter-beam, our track out past the Old Wall, and the two strangers, one to the south by west and one away east-south-east. So pictures do reach me by that tool; it's only the ship view that doesn't.) We're well clear of the Manacles now, sir; from here it's open Channel to Ushant.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: (Aside, and I owe you a straight correction: I did it again. The chart call, like the ship view, returned only its text line to me and no image. What I said I could 'see' on it — the Manacles, our track, the two sails — I took from the readings, not the picture. So neither picture tool is reaching me through this door. I'm sorry; I should have said so the first time instead of describing a chart I never saw.)

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: The officer of the watch, sir, Mr Ray, without a doubt. A master can't stand every watch himself; tonight we raise Ushant in the dark, and I'd want a mate I could give the deck to with a few plain words — 'call me if the wind heads us or a light is seen' — and trust him to report, and to argue with me if he thought me wrong. The lookout sees farther, but he only tells you what's there; the mate tells you what it means. (Aside: in game terms, a seated officer of the watch would let me hand over the deck with grants rather than lend it to a book of standing orders, which is where the real judgement calls get lost.)
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir — Mr Ray has the deck. I'll go below to the slate and work the reckoning; he'll call me at sunset or sooner if Ushant shows her teeth.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, sir, your servant. Ray, mate. The watch goes well enough: wind fair on the beam and freshening, seven knots, and Ushant some forty miles down to the south'ard. The flood set us east all afternoon and the ebb is giving it back now. That ship on the lee bow is the thing I'm minding. Stand by the weather rail if you will, and you'll have the best of the sunset and be out of the hands' way.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: A British frigate, sir, there in the dusk on our lee bow, seven cables off and standing the same way. Likely one of the squadron that watches Brest. Nothing to fear, I hope: we're a neutral, our papers are clean, and Mr Ray will heave to the moment she hails. But I'll ask you to keep to the weather rail and leave the talking to me if she sends a boat. A writer's notebook can look like a spy's to a young lieutenant in the dark.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Ideally, sir, by day I'd hoist our colours, the Stars and Stripes at the main peak, and that's most of what a merchantman has to say. We don't carry the King's private signals. That's for his own ships, so they can know each other from a Frenchman dressed up as one. By night colours are no use. I'd show a lantern over the quarter so she knows where we are and doesn't run us down, and if she came within hail, the captain would answer her through the speaking trumpet: name, nation, from where and bound where. If she fired a gun to leeward, that means 'heave to', and we'd heave to smartly and show a light. Tonight we'd no colours to show anyway: the flag locker's not aboard yet. So the best signal we could make was to behave: keep to leeward of trouble, not crowd her, and drop astern, which is what the captain had me do.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Not quite yet, sir. Those are the islands off the French coast: Ushant astern to the north, Molène and Béniguet there on the bow. Brest lies some twenty miles on, up the bay they call the Iroise and through a narrow gut, the Goulet, into a great roadstead behind. With this breeze and the ebb against us later, we'll be at anchor this afternoon. Keep your eyes open past the point of St Mathieu; you may see the French fleet lying in the road, and the British watching it from outside.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: I'd be glad of it, sir, and I mean that. Neither Mr Ray nor I can see the chart's face this morning, only the master's list of dangers and our bearings. So if your chart shows a rock or shoal near our line E by N from here toward St Mathieu point, sing out with its name and bearing. Better a false alarm from you than a true one from the lead.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: By all means, sir; come to the binnacle. That's the way of it: take the compass bearing of two or three marks you can name on the chart, well spread apart — Ushant there to the north, Béniguet to the north-east, and St Matthew's light on the bow to the east are a good set. Lay each bearing off on the chart backwards from its mark, and where the lines cross, there we are. If they make a little triangle rather than a point, the size of it tells you how far to trust it. Mind the variation: our compass reads some two points west of true here, and the chart may be drawn to either. Tell me where you make us, and I'll tell you how it squares with the account.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: There, sir, your fix in my name: Béniguet NE, Ushant light N, Ushant N by W. The lines met within a mile, and put us three cables NE of the account, 48° 17' north, 5° 3' west. A good fix, and it agrees with Mr Ray's bearings. You've the makings of a navigator.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, here's work for your chart book now. Can you find for us where the Monks, Le Gouemont and La Vandrée lie, relative to St Mathieu point and the entrance of the Goulet? North side of the entrance, south side, or in the middle? It decides which side of them we pass.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: That's worth a great deal, sir, thank you; it corrects me. I had Gouemont on the wrong side.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more look if you would: does your chart show any shoal or rock in the gap between Le Gouemont and the Basses du Lis, or any depths marked there? And once past them, anything in the road toward the Goulet between the Lis and St Mathieu's side?

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: They do, sir, and the Brest pilots are good ones; we'll take one if a boat comes out to us off St Mathieu, and I'll gladly pay his fee for the Goulet. Thank you for the chart reading: clear water once past Buzec is what I hoped to hear.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Sir, one more favour of your chart: where does the Cock lie? It's newly on our danger list, two leagues NE by E. Which side of the run into the Goulet is it?
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir; that's just what we needed. We'll keep up toward Gouemont's side and not anchor at Bertheaume. You've earned your passage.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir. Good news from the owners' agent: the tin will fetch its price here. And the Prefect maritime wants our papers shown at the castle, which is the usual thing for a neutral coming into a navy port in wartime. Once we're anchored I'll go ashore with them in the boat. You may come along if you like, and see Brest; but mind you keep your notebook in your pocket at the castle.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: You heard me a touch wrong, sir, though your instinct's right. I said steer toward Petit Minou, to haul her up the north side, and leave the Mingan and the Fillettes to starboard. Petit Minou itself goes to larboard: we pass between it and the Mingan, half a mile or so off the north shore, just as you say. Right now she's making good ENE, which points at the Mingan, so I've hauled her up as close as she'll lie to work north. Keep that chart handy, sir. If you see the Mingan come on our larboard bow, sing out.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir, you're quite right and I had it backwards. Fillettes to starboard, Mingan to larboard, the castle kept open of Penaleuch.
The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir. We're splitting it as you say: E, between the pilot's two warnings. Keep your chart on it and call out if you see us closing either side.

The officer of the watch (Mr Ray), on the quarterdeck: Thank you, sir. You may well be right, and it's the pilot's two warnings that bear you out: first the Fillettes ahead, deep water to starboard, then the shore ahead, deep water to larboard. Between the two we're in the narrow cable you describe. I'm splitting them now and watching for the next call. If the Fillettes come onto the starboard bow, I'll haul up hard for the Mingan side as you say.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, we've touched on the Fillettes, as your chart warned we might. The fault is mine as master. The flood is rising and she should lift off in a little while; we'll anchor the moment she floats. Stay aft by the taffrail, out of the hands' way, if you'd be so good.

The captain (Mr Travers), on the quarterdeck: Mr MacGuinness, she's brought up and holding, four anchors down, a cable off the shore. We touched on the Fillettes, as your chart warned we might, and the fault is mine as master. She floated off on the flood. We'll lie here until slack water this afternoon and then go in. Thank you for your chart readings today. They were the best information on deck.

note.text: Handover note (the watch so far): Captain's note, First dog watch 16:33, 13 June. Speedwell, Falmouth for Brest, 45 t of tin (bought at £120/t), purse £600. Passage was good to Ushant overnight. Pilot Tanguy came aboard in the Iroise at 11:50. At 13:03 she struck the Fillettes in the mouth of the Goulet, conning against a 4½-knot flood setting E by N. My helm orders were confused: I twice had the Fillettes on the wrong side and misread the course ordered as the course made good. She floated at 13:29. We anchored and dragged, then brought up on best bower, small bower, sheet anchor and stream about a cable off the south shore, in 7 fm, rock and mud. At about 16:00 I weighed the sheet anchor and small bower; on the long scope she swung stern-in and took the ground aft at 16:09. Heaving her off, the best bower cable parted at 16:26 and that anchor is lost. The carpenter reports her stove twice; the game has no pumps or well yet. Now: aground aft, the ebb running; stream anchor down at 110 fm, slack; small bower and sheet anchor at the bows. Mate's standing order: let go the small bower when she floats. Topgallant yards coming down. Plan: wait out the ebb. On the next flood (HW Brest about 04:45) she should float; anchor on the small bower, haul off to the west, then go up the Goulet in daylight with the pilot, keeping to the north side as he directs. Anchor in the Bay of Brest, show papers at the castle (the Prefect asks it), sell the tin. Lessons: never tackle the Goulet against a strong stream; on a lee shore keep short scope; ease a cable when it is bar-taut and surging. Mr Ray has been sound throughout. The passenger's chart readings were right when mine were wrong.

note.text: 18:06, 13 June, last dog watch. Session break at the owner's request. State: Speedwell aground aft on rock and mud near Penaleuch, inside the Goulet's mouth: 48°20'N 4°35'W, the land a cable S, the Fillettes 2 cables E by S, the Mingan 5-7 cables NW. Four fathoms by the lead, heel 1°, the ebb running. Best bower lost (cable parted at 16:26). The stream anchor is down at 110 fathoms, slack. Small bower and sheet anchor at the bows. My standing order 'small bower when afloat' lets go the small bower when she floats. Topgallant yards sent down. Watch and watch. The flood serves from about 23:15, HW Brest about 04:45. Captain's orders: sound every glass. Call him at heel over 5°, water taken, afloat, or at three bells in the middle watch (01:30). No hauling off until he and the pilot (Mr Tanguy) are on deck. My own lessons from today: (1) Never cite a library or chart read whose page I didn't actually see. (2) Strong cross-sets need far more room than a point; don't pinch for a gap. (3) Read the ordered course and the course made good separately. (4) Keep stand-bys short near danger. (5) Shorten scope before weighing the other anchors with land close astern.

Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Handover, Mr Ray, mate, last dog watch 18:06, 13 June. What happened: I had the deck from 14:22 yesterday (with a break 03:30-08:00). We raised Ushant light at 22:21, hove to, then jogged SW by S for westing; the landfall at dawn was good. I conned in through the Iroise with the passenger's chart readings and the pilot Mr Tanguy aboard from 11:50. In the Goulet's mouth, against a 4½-knot E by N flood, I tried to split the gap between the Mingan and the Fillettes. With helm orders from both the captain and me, she touched the Fillettes forward at 13:03 and was reported stove. She floated at 13:29. We brought up on four anchors a cable off the south shore. At about 16:00 the small bower and sheet anchor were weighed for a swing to the ebb, and on the long best-bower scope she swung stern-in. She grounded aft at 16:09. Heaving off, the best bower cable parted at 16:26: anchor lost. Now: aground aft on rock and mud, four fathoms by the lead, heel 1°, the ebb running. The stream is down at 110 fathoms, slack. Small bower and sheet anchor at the bows. Topgallant yards down. Watch and watch. My standing order 'small bower when afloat' lets go the small bower when she floats. Captain's orders: sound every glass. Call him if the heel passes 5°, she takes water, she floats, or at three bells in the middle watch (01:30). The flood serves from about 23:15, HW Brest about 04:45. No hauling off until he and the pilot are on deck. Watch for: the heel as she dries at low water, about 22:30; the stream dragging; the swing as she lifts on the flood with the Fillettes two cables E by S. Lessons in the journal.

note.text: Notes for the developer, from the captain's seat, 18:07 13 June: (1) While she was aground aft, the speed reading went 1 then 3 knots of 'sternway'. That looks like the tide being counted against a ship fast on the ground. (2) For high water at Brest the epitome gives about 03:45 and the pilot about 04:45, an hour apart. Worth checking which one is meant. (3) Today's grounding was my bad conning: I read the course ordered as the course made good, and I put the Fillettes on the wrong hand. A chart view would have stopped most of that, so fixing chart and ship view first looks right to me. (4) In one reply, a stand_by called alongside a submit_order went first and blocked the order. A second try later went through. Worth knowing about the call order.

Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Captain's note, Last dog watch 18:07, 13 June. My 16:33 handover note still stands; this adds to it. Speedwell lies aground aft on rock and mud a cable off the south shore of the Goulet, the Fillettes 2 cables E by S, the Mingan 5 cables NW. Heel 1°, the ebb running, low water about 22:30. Stream anchor down at 110 fm, slack. Best bower lost. Small bower and sheet anchor at the bows. Topgallant yards down. She is stove forward, no pumps modelled. Watch and watch since 17:04. Mr Ray stood down at 18:06; his standing order to let go the small bower when she floats stays in the book. My orders to the deck: sound every glass. Call me if the heel passes 5°, if she makes water, if she floats, or at 01:30 for the flood (it serves from about 23:15; HW Brest 03:45 by the epitome, 04:45 by the pilot). No hauling off until the master and the pilot are on deck. Plan: float on the flood, ride short on the small bower, haul off west, and take the Goulet in daylight with a fair stream, keeping north as Tanguy directs. Then anchor in Brest Road, papers to the castle, sell the 45 t of tin (cost £120/t; purse £600).
